summary.text: Define \(u_0=-2,\ u_1=-56\) and \(u_{n+2}=-4u_{n+1}-64u_n\); expanding this recurrence shows that \(u_n^2\) satisfies \(v_{n+3}=-48v_{n+2}+3072v_{n+1}+262144v_n\). The original fourth-order recurrence gives the same stride-two recurrence for the odd-indexed terms, and the first three values agree, so induction yields \(a(2n+1)=u_n^2\) for all \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that every odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is the square of an integer.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
u_0=-2,\qquad u_1=-56,
\]
and
\[
u_{r+2}=-4u_{r+1}-64u_r\qquad(r\ge 0).
\tag{2}
\]
We will prove the more precise identity
\[
a_{2n+1}=u_n^2
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(n\ge 0\).

First, we derive a recurrence involving every second term of \(a\). We claim that for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+6}=-48a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}+262144a_r.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, applying (1) at indices \(r+6\) and \(r+5\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{r+6}
  &= -4a_{r+5}+256a_{r+3}+4096a_{r+2},\\
a_{r+5}
  &= -4a_{r+4}+256a_{r+2}+4096a_{r+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution of the second equation into the first yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{r+6}
 &= -4\bigl(-4a_{r+4}+256a_{r+2}+4096a_{r+1}\bigr)
       +256a_{r+3}+4096a_{r+2}\\
 &=16a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}+256a_{r+3}-16384a_{r+1}.
\tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
A further application of (1), now at index \(r+4\), says
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\]
Multiplying this equality by \(-64\), and then rearranging, gives
\[
256a_{r+3}-16384a_{r+1}=-64a_{r+4}+262144a_r.
\tag{6}
\]
Inserting (6) into (5), we obtain
\[
a_{r+6}
 =16a_{r+4}+3072a_{r+2}-64a_{r+4}+262144a_r,
\]
which is exactly (4).

Next, we show that the squares of the auxiliary sequence satisfy the same recurrence. We claim that for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
u_{r+3}^2=-48u_{r+2}^2+3072u_{r+1}^2+262144u_r^2.
\tag{7}
\]
To verify this, put \(x=u_r\) and \(y=u_{r+1}\). By (2),
\[
u_{r+2}=-4y-64x,
\]
and therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{r+3}
  &=-4u_{r+2}-64u_{r+1}\\
  &=-4(-4y-64x)-64y\\
  &=256x-48y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
u_{r+3}^2=(256x-48y)^2
 =65536x^2-24576xy+2304y^2.
\tag{8}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
-48u_{r+2}^2+3072u_{r+1}^2+262144u_r^2
 &=-48(-4y-64x)^2+3072y^2+262144x^2\\
 &=-48(16y^2+512xy+4096x^2)
      +3072y^2+262144x^2\\
 &=2304y^2-24576xy+65536x^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This agrees with (8), proving (7).

It remains to establish (3). We first check the three initial cases.

For \(n=0\),
\[
a_{2\cdot0+1}=a_1=4=(-2)^2=u_0^2.
\]
For \(n=1\),
\[
a_{2\cdot1+1}=a_3=3136=(-56)^2=u_1^2.
\]
For the third case, (2) gives
\[
u_2=-4u_1-64u_0=-4(-56)-64(-2)=224+128=352.
\]
We compute the needed term of \(a\) from (1). First,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
 &=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
 &=-4(3136)+256(4)+4096(-1)\\
 &=-15616.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
 &=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
 &=-4(-15616)+256(176)+4096(4)\\
 &=62464+45056+16384\\
 &=123904\\
 &=352^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a_5=u_2^2\), proving (3) for \(n=2\).

We now proceed by strong induction on \(n\). The cases \(n=0,1,2\) have just been proved. Suppose \(n=k+3\) for some \(k\ge 0\), and suppose the identity is already known at the three smaller indices \(k,k+1,k+2\). Apply (4) with \(r=2k+1\). Since
\[
(2k+1)+6=2(k+3)+1,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2(k+3)+1}
 &= -48a_{(2k+1)+4}+3072a_{(2k+1)+2}+262144a_{2k+1}\\
 &= -48a_{2(k+2)+1}+3072a_{2(k+1)+1}+262144a_{2k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the induction hypotheses at \(k+2\), \(k+1\), and \(k\), respectively, this becomes
\[
a_{2(k+3)+1}
 =-48u_{k+2}^2+3072u_{k+1}^2+262144u_k^2.
\]
By the square recurrence (7), the right-hand side is \(u_{k+3}^2\). Hence
\[
a_{2(k+3)+1}=u_{k+3}^2,
\]
which completes the induction and proves (3) for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

Finally, each \(u_n\) is an integer, so (3) explicitly exhibits \(a_{2n+1}\) as the square of the integer \(u_n\). Therefore \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
